title: Servants’ Green
subtitle: The Legend of Lucien Vaire
teaser: He learned the sword through a window and lost his first duel headfirst into a barrel of eels. Then a woman who hated noblemen even more than he did made him an offer: she would teach him everything, for half of everything he ever won.

sections.heading: I. The Window
paragraphs: Lucien Vaire learned to fence through a window.

The Salle Ysolde stood on the Quai des Lames in Saint-Ombre, a port city where even the fishwives carried knives and the dukes settled their quarrels before breakfast. Every noble heir in the city learned the sword there. On the ledge of its third window, most afternoons, lay a skinny blond boy with a dirty face and somebody else’s purse down his shirt.
He was twelve, and a pickpocket, and the salle was the best hunting in the city. None of the young lords ever looked at a gutter boy long enough to remember his face.
After a while, he stopped coming for the purses.

Inside, under the chandeliers, the heirs of Saint-Ombre lunged in white canvas while an old woman with a voice like a cracked bell told them they were useless. Lucien learned the words before he knew what they meant. Prise de fer: take the iron. Coup droit: the straight blow. At night, on the roofs above the fish market, he did them with a broom handle against the laundry lines until his arm shook.

One heir he watched above all: Octave d’Aubreval, the duke’s son, academy champion at fifteen, tall, fair and bored. He fenced like a man signing his name, one quick, elegant line, and the other boy was on the floor. When he won, he tossed his foil over his shoulder without looking to see if anyone caught it.
Somebody always did. That was what it meant to be Octave d’Aubreval.
Lucien hated him completely, and studied him like scripture.

sections.heading: II. The Fish Market
paragraphs: At sixteen, Lucien stole a rapier.

It belonged to a harbour lieutenant passed out drunk in a tavern doorway, and it was the most beautiful thing Lucien had ever held: a swept hilt like a cage of silver vines. Next morning he climbed onto a crate in the fish market, where the Aubreval carriage stopped every Thursday for oysters, and pointed the sword at its door.
“Octave d’Aubreval! I challenge you!”
The market went quiet. Octave stepped down and looked him over: the bare feet, the torn shirt, the stolen sword.
“On what grounds?”
Lucien had not thought about grounds. “On the grounds that I can beat you.”

Octave laughed. He drew, swept a low and perfect court bow, the kind the nobles of Saint-Ombre made to one another at the Midsummer Ball, and held out his free hand like a gentleman inviting a lady onto the floor.
“Then, mademoiselle,” he said, “shall we dance?”
The fishwives shrieked.

It took about as long as a song. Lucien threw everything he had stolen through the window, and Octave met all of it without moving his feet. Then his point flicked out and a button flew off Lucien’s shirt. Then another, and another, while the market counted them aloud. When the shirt fell open, Octave took the rapier out of Lucien’s hand like a spoon from a baby, smacked him across the backside with the flat, and sent him off the crate headfirst into a barrel of live eels.
When he came up spitting, Octave flipped a silver coin into the barrel.
“For the lesson,” he said, and climbed back into his carriage.
Lucien crawled out with the whole market laughing, the coin in his fist. He never spent it. He wore it on a string around his neck.

sections.heading: III. Half of Everything
paragraphs: Master Ysolde found him the next night, on the roof above her own windows.
She was sixty-one, a ropemaker’s daughter who had become the finest sword in Saint-Ombre. She came up the drainpipe without a sound, sat on the ridge tiles, and lit a pipe.
“I watched you lose,” she said. “You lost like an idiot. But you lost in my style. So you’re a thief.”
“I never took anything from you.”
“You took four thousand crowns’ worth of lessons. That’s what the Duke of Aubreval has paid me for his boy so far.” She blew smoke at the moon. “Can you pay?”
“No.”

“Then here is my offer, and I make it once. You sweep my floors by day, in my livery. You fence by night, when I say, against whom I say. And when you start winning purses, half of everything you win is mine. For the rest of your life.”
“That’s robbery.”
“That’s business. Charity is for people who can afford to be wrong. Yes or no?”

So he swept her floors. The salle dressed its servants in a cheap bottle green so nobody would mistake them for students, and for three years Lucien wore it, fetching towels for the heirs of Saint-Ombre and scrubbing their blood off the boards.

At night she taught him, and she was not kind about it. She made him hold his guard with a full cup of wine on his wrist until he could do it for an hour without spilling, and then she drank the wine.

“The nobles fence the way they dance,” she told him. “Lovely to watch, every step announced. So give them flourishes. Wave your sword about like a peacock. Let them watch the pretty thing. Then take the blade and go straight.”

She taught him the prise de fer, the parry that doesn’t block a sword but takes it and leads it away. “Don’t fight their iron. Take it. It’s the only thing a nobleman ever lets go of.” Then the coup droit that follows: the straight thrust down the open line, so plain and so fast that nobody has time to be insulted by it.

When he was ready, she began booking her students private lessons at midnight. They arrived to find the floor boy waiting with a foil, and they lost, every one, and none could tell a soul. Beaten by the boy who mopped up after him? One young viscount paid Lucien ten crowns to keep quiet.
Ysolde took five.
“Why are you really doing this?” he asked her once.

“Six of my students have won the Queen’s Tournament,” she said. “Six times I watched from the cheap seats, because the Houses don’t seat a fencing master in the royal stand. They seat her with the help.” She tapped his green sleeve with the stem of her pipe. “Before I die, I’d like to watch the help take one of their swords away.”

sections.heading: IV. The Queen’s Tournament
paragraphs: The Queen’s Tournament was the oldest contest in Saint-Ombre, and its first rule was older than the city walls: every fencer fights in the colours of his house.
There had never been a second rule. No commoner had ever been mad enough to need one.
When the herald read out Lucien’s name, a young lord in the royal stand called down, “And which house does the floor boy fence for?”
Ysolde stood up in the cheap seats. “Mine.”

The judges spent an hour with the charter and found no word against it. So Lucien Vaire walked into the ring in servants’ green, the colour of every scullion and footman in the city, and a roar began in the cheap seats and rolled down over the nobles like a wave.

He won his first bout with a flourish so ridiculous that the crowd cheered before the touch landed. By the fifth day a man was selling green ribbons outside the gates, and by the final half the city wore them.

The final was against Octave d’Aubreval, twice the Queen’s champion now and far better than he had been in the fish market. The boredom was gone. He had seen the ribbons, and for the first time in his life he wanted something he did not already have.
Before the herald could call them on, Lucien swept a low and perfect court bow and held out his free hand.
“Then, my lord,” he said, “shall we dance?”
Octave went white, then red.

It was the finest fight Saint-Ombre had ever seen. Octave came on like a squall, every thrust meant to finish it. Lucien gave him a show. He spun under a cut. He let the green coat flare so Octave’s point went through cloth instead of ribs. He flourished and feinted and grinned up at the royal stand, and every time Octave’s eyes followed the pretty thing, a little more of his temper went with them.
On the fourteenth pass, Octave lunged in a fury, and Lucien took the iron.

The prise de fer bound the blade and carried it wide, and Octave’s sword went spinning over the barrier into the royal stand. A footman caught it. Somebody always did. Lucien’s coup droit came straight down the open line and stopped with its point on the top button of Octave’s doublet.
He flicked it off.
Then he lifted the old silver coin from the string around his neck and tossed it to the duke’s son.
“For the lesson,” he said.

The cheap seats came over the barrier. At the very top of them, Master Ysolde sat perfectly still with her pipe cold in her teeth, doing sums. A man near her swore afterwards that she was smiling, but nobody believed him.
Lucien won it again the next year, and the year after that.

sections.heading: V. The Green Flourish
paragraphs: After the third, the Queen offered him a knighthood.
It was the Houses’ idea. If Lucien Vaire became the Chevalier de Vaire, then a nobleman had won three years running, and the world was as it had always been. He would never have to wear green again.
He thought about it for exactly as long as it took to bow.
“Your Majesty is too generous,” he said. “But a title would only ruin the cape.”

By then it was a cape: the old livery, cut and lengthened into a great sweeping thing that swirled when he turned, the most expensive servant’s coat in the history of Saint-Ombre. The Queen laughed. The Houses did not. The next spring they gave the Tournament its second rule at last: entrants must be of noble birth.
They had changed the rules rather than lose to him again. Lucien considered it the greatest compliment of his life.

So he took his sword to the duelling rings, where nobody asks who your father was, only whether you can still stand. He likes opponents with crests on their shields best, and always gives them the show first: the flourishes, the feints, the green cape flaring like a flag. He lets them watch the pretty thing. Then he takes their iron and goes straight.

Half of every purse still goes to the Salle Ysolde. She has never written to thank him. She has, however, nailed a sign beside the tall windows in the alley, where gutter boys still lie on the ledges to watch. It says: WATCHING, TWO COPPERS. Nobody has ever seen her collect. Lucien has never asked. Some questions are bad for business.
They call him the Green Flourish now. The nobles call him other things, quietly.

Before every fight he sweeps the same low court bow he first saw from the top of a fish crate, and holds out his free hand like a gentleman at the Midsummer Ball. It is the politest thing anyone will say to you in the ring. It is also a promise that somewhere in the next minute, he is going to take something you were born with and give it to the cheap seats.
